```{r load}
# data from data-raw/vignette_chinook.R
vd <- function(f) system.file("vignette-data", f, package = "knowledge", mustWork = TRUE)
x <- readRDS(vd("chinook_rearing.rds"))
seg <- readRDS(vd("bulk_segments.rds"))
water <- readRDS(vd("bulk_water.rds"))
fp_grade <- terra::rast(vd("bulk_fp_grade.tif")) / 100

tune <- x$tune
summ <- x$summary
meta <- x$meta
cmp <- x$compare
dflt <- tune[tune$is_default, ]
rec <- tune[tune$recommended %in% TRUE, ]
region <- tune[tune$in_region, ]
all_row <- cmp[cmp$watershed_group_code == "ALL", ]
per_group <- cmp[cmp$watershed_group_code != "ALL", ]
map_row <- cmp[cmp$watershed_group_code == meta$map_group, ]

# formatting
n0 <- function(v) format(round(v), big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE, trim = TRUE)
n1 <- function(v) format(round(v, 1), big.mark = ",", nsmall = 1, scientific = FALSE, trim = TRUE)
pc <- function(v, d = 0) paste0(formatC(100 * v, format = "f", digits = d), " %")
grad <- function(g) paste0(signif(100 * g, 3), " %")
km_d <- function(d) if (d >= 1000) paste(format(d / 1000, trim = TRUE), "km") else paste(d, "m")
words <- function(r) {
  size <- if (r$size_var == "mad") sprintf("MAD at least %s m³/s", format(r$size_min, trim = TRUE))
          else sprintf("channel width at least %s m", format(r$size_min, trim = TRUE))
  exc <- if (is.na(r$exc_q)) "no exception"
         else sprintf("or a river of at least %s m³/s within %s downstream", r$exc_q, km_d(r$exc_d))
  sprintf("gradient at most %s, and %s %s", grad(r$grad_max), size, exc)
}
lst <- function(v, and = "and") if (length(v) < 2) v else paste(paste(v[-length(v)], collapse = ", "), and, v[length(v)])
short <- function(r) {
  size <- if (r$size_var == "mad") paste0("MAD ≥ ", r$size_min) else paste0("width ≥ ", r$size_min, " m")
  exc <- if (is.na(r$exc_q)) "no exception" else paste0(r$exc_q, " m³/s within ", km_d(r$exc_d))
  paste0(size, ", ≤ ", grad(r$grad_max), ", ", exc)
}
fold_n <- table(x$groups$fold)
honest <- x$honest
seeds <- x$seeds
share_of <- function(col, v) sum(tune$boot_rec_share[tune[[col]] %in% v])
no_grad <- function(rule) sub("\\|g<=[0-9.]+\\|", "|", rule)
```

link draws chinook rearing habitat as a yes or a no on every stream segment, from a size floor
and a gradient maximum. This article follows, for someone who has not seen the work, how the
province's electrofishing record was used to choose between `r n0(nrow(tune))` versions of
that rule, how firm the choice is, and what the chosen rule changes on the ground. Every number
is read from the tables the tuning wrote.

The recommended rule, in one line: **`r words(rec)`**.

## What does link draw for chinook rearing now?

link's `default` configuration marks a segment as chinook rearing habitat when the segment is
accessible to chinook and one of four tests holds:

- **stream**: a stream edge with a gradient of at most `r grad(dflt$grad_max)` and a channel
  width of at least `r dflt$size_min` m;
- **river**: inside a river polygon, at the same gradient, with any width;
- **wetland**: inside a wetland of at least 1 ha;
- **lake**: inside a lake of at least 100 ha.

Three passes follow. Known reaches entered by hand are set. Rearing that has no spawning within
10 km is removed. Lake and wetland rearing must connect to spawning.

Channel width is modelled only on streams of order 2 and up, so the stream test never admits an
unmeasured first-order stream. That matters below, because the rule this article recommends
can.

The tuning asks about the stream test only. River polygons keep their size test, and wetlands
and lakes keep theirs, under every rule. River polygons share the stream test's gradient
maximum in link's configuration, so that one value moves with it.

## Which rules were asked about?

Each candidate rule changes three parts of the stream test, starting from `default`'s:

- **a size test**: a floor on mean annual discharge (MAD, the modelled average flow) of
  `r lst(sort(unique(tune$size_min[tune$size_var == "mad"])), "or")` m³/s, or a floor on channel
  width of `r lst(sort(unique(tune$size_min[tune$size_var == "width"])), "or")` m;
- **a gradient maximum** of `r lst(grad(sort(unique(tune$grad_max))), "or")`;
- **an exception**: none, or a segment that fails the size test still counts when a river of at
  least Q m³/s lies within D m downstream, with Q one of
  `r lst(sort(unique(na.omit(tune$exc_q))), "or")` m³/s and D one of
  `r lst(format(sort(unique(na.omit(tune$exc_d))), big.mark = ",", trim = TRUE), "or")` m.

Every combination is one rule: `r length(unique(paste(tune$size_var, tune$size_min)))` size
tests, `r length(unique(tune$grad_max))` gradients and
`r length(unique(paste(tune$exc_q, tune$exc_d)))` exception settings make
`r n0(nrow(tune))` rules. `default` is one of them: width at least `r dflt$size_min` m,
`r grad(dflt$grad_max)`, no exception.

The exception exists because chinook juveniles move up out of large rivers into small streams
close to them. A small stream next to a large river can hold them when a small stream far from
one does not.

## What evidence scores a rule?

The evidence is the provincial Fisheries Data Information System (FDIS) electrofishing export:
site visits with what was caught, placed on link's stream segments. A visit counts towards
chinook rearing when it is on a stream edge outside river polygons, wetlands of 1 ha or more and
lakes of 100 ha or more. Its fished area must be 10 to 10,000 m², in a watershed group where link
marks chinook present. It must carry no record code that could hide chinook, and have no natural
chinook barrier downstream. That leaves `r n0(summ$visits_in)` visits in `r summ$groups` groups,
`r n0(summ$detections)` of which caught chinook.

A group where chinook were never caught, or caught on every visit, cannot tell one rule from
another, so the models use the `r summ$groups_both` groups with both outcomes:
**`r n0(dflt$n_visits)` visits and `r n0(dflt$n_detect)` detections**. Every count below is on
these visits unless it says otherwise.

Each visit carries what link would read at that spot:

- the gradient of its Freshwater Atlas segment;
- the channel width link would use on a stream nobody measured, never the width measured on the
  visit itself;
- the modelled MAD;
- the distance downstream to the first river of each size Q, on the same flow.

## How is a rule scored?

A rule splits the visits into those it calls habitat and those it does not. The question is
whether that split predicts where chinook are caught in watersheds the model has not seen.

1. A model of the chance of catching chinook on a visit takes the fished area, the data set, the
   era and the watershed group into account, and adds the rule as one more term: in or out.
2. The `r summ$groups_both` groups are dealt into `r meta$spec$folds` folds of
   `r lst(as.integer(fold_n))` groups, balanced by detections. The model is fitted on four folds
   and predicts the visits of the fifth, so each group is held out once.
3. The score is the held-out deviance: how surprised the model is, in total, by the visits it
   did not see. Lower is better. A rule that sorts caught from not-caught visits in a new
   watershed scores low.
4. Each rule is compared with the best one group by group. The standard error (SE) of the
   difference is taken over groups, because a watershed group, not a visit, is the unit that
   repeats.

The model with no rule term at all scores `r n1(rec$ddev_null * -1)` above the best rule. That
is the range a rule can move the score.

## Which rules can the data not tell apart?

A rule is in the **region** when its score is within one SE of the best. The data cannot rank
the rules inside it. `r nrow(region)` rules are in it, and they share one shape:

- every one sizes streams by flow, with a MAD floor of
  `r min(region$size_min)` to `r max(region$size_min)` m³/s;
- every one has the exception, with a river of `r min(region$exc_q)` to `r max(region$exc_q)`
  m³/s within `r km_d(min(region$exc_d))` to `r km_d(max(region$exc_d))`;
- every one has a gradient maximum of `r lst(grad(sort(unique(region$grad_max))), "or")`.

`default` is `r n1(dflt$ddev_best)` above the best rule, with an SE of `r n1(dflt$se_diff)`, so
it is outside. So is every rule without the exception: the best of them is
`r n1(min(tune$ddev_best[is.na(tune$exc_q)]))` above the best. So is every width rule: the best
is `r n1(min(tune$ddev_best[tune$size_var == "width"]))` above.

```{r profile, fig.height = 5.2, fig.cap = "How far each value of each part of the rule can get from the best score. Each point is the best score of any rule with that value, as deviance above the best rule; lower is better. A filled point has at least one rule in the region. A ring marks `default`'s value."}
comp <- function(lab, v, key) {
  tune |>
    mutate(value = v) |>
    group_by(value, key = key) |>
    summarise(best = min(ddev_best), in_region = any(in_region), is_default = any(is_default), .groups = "drop") |>
    mutate(part = lab)
}
size_lab <- paste(ifelse(tune$size_var == "mad", "MAD", "width"), as.character(tune$size_min))
size_key <- ifelse(tune$size_var == "mad", tune$size_min, 10 + tune$size_min)
prof <- bind_rows(
  comp("Size test (m³/s or m)", size_lab, size_key),
  comp("Gradient maximum", grad(tune$grad_max), tune$grad_max),
  comp("Exception: river size Q (m³/s)", ifelse(is.na(tune$exc_q), "none", format(tune$exc_q, trim = TRUE)),
       ifelse(is.na(tune$exc_q), -1, tune$exc_q)),
  comp("Exception: distance D (m)", ifelse(is.na(tune$exc_d), "none", format(tune$exc_d, big.mark = ",", trim = TRUE)),
       ifelse(is.na(tune$exc_d), -1, tune$exc_d))
)
prof$part <- factor(prof$part, levels = unique(prof$part))
prof <- prof |> group_by(part) |> mutate(value = factor(value, levels = unique(value[order(key)]))) |> ungroup()
dflt_vals <- tibble(
  part = factor(levels(prof$part), levels = levels(prof$part)),
  value = c(paste("width", as.character(dflt$size_min)), grad(dflt$grad_max), "none", "none")
)
dpts <- inner_join(prof, dflt_vals, by = c("part", "value"))
ggplot(prof, aes(value, best)) +
  geom_line(aes(group = 1), colour = "grey70") +
  geom_point(aes(fill = in_region), shape = 21, size = 2.6, colour = "grey20") +
  geom_point(data = dpts, shape = 21, size = 5, stroke = 1, colour = "#d95f02", fill = NA) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "#1b6ca8", `FALSE` = "white"),
                    labels = c(`TRUE` = "a rule in the region", `FALSE` = "none in the region"), name = NULL) +
  facet_wrap(~part, scales = "free_x", ncol = 2) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Deviance above the best rule") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1), legend.position = "bottom",
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```

## Which rule is recommended, and why?

Before any rule was scored, the choice was fixed as: the rule in the region that departs from
`default` in the fewest parts, and among those the best scorer. Every rule in the region departs
from `default` in all three parts, so the best scorer is recommended:

> **`r words(rec)`**.

One more condition was fixed in advance. An exception distance under
`r meta$spec$d_floor` m would be moved off, because so close to a river a stream visit cannot be
told from a catch in the river snapped to the tributary's mouth. The recommended distance is
`r km_d(rec$exc_d)`, so it stands.

The recommended rule is narrower than `default`, not wider. It calls fewer visits habitat and
takes in as many catches:

```{r raw}
raw <- bind_rows(dflt, rec) |>
  transmute(Rule = c("`default`", "recommended"),
            `Visits in` = n0(n_in), `Detections in` = n0(n_detect_in),
            `Rate in` = pc(raw_rate_in, 1), `Rate out` = pc(raw_rate_out, 1))
knitr::kable(raw, align = "lrrrr",
             caption = paste0("What the two rules call habitat on the ", n0(dflt$n_visits),
                              " visits the models use: visits and chinook detections in, and the share of visits ",
                              "that caught chinook in and out."))
```

The exception is not mainly a way of adding streams. It is what lets a higher size floor keep the
small streams beside a river, where chinook are caught.

## How firm is the choice?

Three checks were fixed before the run.

**More fold seeds.** Dealing the groups into folds is random. Dealt `r nrow(seeds)` more ways,
`r sum(seeds$recommended == rec$rule)` of `r nrow(seeds)` recommend the same rule, and the
recommended rule is in the region of `r sum(seeds$main_rec_in_region)` of them. `default` is in
`r sum(seeds$default_in_region)`. `r sum(seeds$recommended != rec$rule & no_grad(seeds$recommended) == no_grad(rec$rule))` of them differ from it only in the gradient. Each seed's recommendation:

```{r seeds}
seed_rules <- tune[match(seeds$recommended, tune$rule), ]
knitr::kable(tibble(Seed = seeds$seed, `Recommended` = vapply(seq_len(nrow(seed_rules)), function(i) words(seed_rules[i, ]), ""),
                    `Rules in its region` = seeds$region_n),
             caption = "The recommendation on each of the extra fold seeds.")
```

**Choosing and scoring on different groups.** The region and the pick above use every group. To
see whether choosing a rule on the same data it is scored on flatters it, the choice was made
on four folds and scored on the fifth, once per fold:

```{r honest}
hk <- tibble(Fold = honest$fold, Groups = honest$n_wsg,
             `Rule chosen on the other four` = vapply(match(honest$rule, tune$rule), function(i) short(tune[i, ]), ""),
             `Chosen` = n1(honest$dev_rec), `default` = n1(honest$dev_default), `No rule` = n1(honest$dev_null))
hk <- bind_rows(hk, tibble(Fold = NA, Groups = sum(honest$n_wsg), `Rule chosen on the other four` = "total",
                           `Chosen` = n1(sum(honest$dev_rec)), `default` = n1(sum(honest$dev_default)),
                           `No rule` = n1(sum(honest$dev_null))))
hk$Fold <- ifelse(is.na(hk$Fold), "", hk$Fold)
knitr::kable(hk, align = "rrlrrr",
             caption = "Held-out deviance on each fold of the rule chosen on the other four, beside `default` and the model with no rule term. Lower is better.")
```

```{r honest-lose}
lose <- honest[honest$dev_rec > honest$dev_default, ]
```

The chosen rule beats `default` in total, `r n1(sum(honest$dev_rec))` against
`r n1(sum(honest$dev_default))`. It loses in `r nrow(lose)` of the `r nrow(honest)` folds: fold
`r lose$fold`, by `r n1(lose$dev_rec - lose$dev_default)`. Every fold's choice sizes streams by
flow and carries the exception.

**Resampling the groups.** Drawing the groups again with replacement `r meta$spec$n_boot` times
and repeating the choice, the recommended rule comes out in `r pc(rec$boot_rec_share)` of draws
and is in the region in `r pc(rec$boot_region_share)`. Its parts are more stable than the rule as
a whole:

- MAD at least `r rec$size_min` m³/s in `r pc(share_of("size_min", rec$size_min))` of draws, and a
  MAD floor of some size in `r pc(sum(tune$boot_rec_share[tune$size_var == "mad"]))`;
- a river of at least `r rec$exc_q` m³/s for the exception in
  `r pc(share_of("exc_q", rec$exc_q))`;
- a distance of `r km_d(rec$exc_d)` in `r pc(share_of("exc_d", rec$exc_d))`, and
  `r km_d(2000)` in `r pc(share_of("exc_d", 2000))`;
- a gradient maximum of `r grad(rec$grad_max)` in `r pc(share_of("grad_max", rec$grad_max))`,
  `r grad(0.07)` in `r pc(share_of("grad_max", 0.07))` and `default`'s `r grad(dflt$grad_max)` in
  `r pc(share_of("grad_max", dflt$grad_max))`.

The shape is settled: a flow floor near 0.75 m³/s and an exception for streams near a river of
about 3 m³/s. The gradient maximum is the least settled part.

An earlier tuning of the same rules, on the 55 groups link had run by then, recommended the
same shape at a gradient of 7 %.

## How does the chance of a catch change across each threshold?

After the choice, one smooth model of detection was fitted on the same visits: stream size and
distance to a `r rec$exc_q` m³/s river together, gradient on its own, with the same other terms.
Each curve below holds the other two at reference values and is shown relative to the chance at
the recommended threshold.

```{r curves, fig.height = 3.4, fig.cap = "The chance of catching chinook on a visit against stream size, gradient and distance to a river, relative to the chance at the recommended threshold (dashed), with its 95 % band. Size and distance are on log scales."}
one_curve <- function(cname, xlab, log_x) {
  d <- x$curves[x$curves$curve == cname, ]
  if (cname == "size_mad") d <- d[d$x >= 0.01, ]
  p <- ggplot(d, aes(x, rel_rate)) +
    geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = rel_lo, ymax = rel_hi), fill = "#c6dbef") +
    geom_line(colour = "#08306b") +
    geom_vline(xintercept = d$threshold[1], linetype = "dashed", colour = "#d95f02") +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 1, colour = "grey60") +
    scale_y_log10(breaks = 10^(-3:2), labels = c("0.001", "0.01", "0.1", "1", "10", "100")) +
    coord_cartesian(ylim = c(1e-3, 1e2)) +
    labs(x = xlab, y = if (cname == "size_mad") "Chance relative to the threshold's" else NULL) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 9) +
    theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
  if (log_x) p + scale_x_log10(labels = function(v) format(v, big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE, drop0trailing = TRUE))
  else p + scale_x_continuous(labels = function(v) paste0(100 * v, " %"))
}
grid::grid.newpage()
grid::pushViewport(grid::viewport(layout = grid::grid.layout(1, 3)))
ps <- list(one_curve("size_mad", "MAD (m³/s)", TRUE), one_curve("gradient", "Gradient", FALSE),
           one_curve("dist_to_Q3_m", "Distance to the river (m)", TRUE))
for (i in 1:3) print(ps[[i]], vp = grid::viewport(layout.pos.row = 1, layout.pos.col = i))
```

```{r curve-points}
at <- function(cname, v) {
  d <- x$curves[x$curves$curve == cname, ]
  stats::approx(log(d$x), d$rel_rate, xout = log(v))$y
}
```

```{r dist-peak}
dc <- x$curves[x$curves$curve == "dist_to_Q3_m", ]
peak_m <- dc$x[which.max(dc$rel_rate)]
```

Flow and gradient have no bend at their thresholds. The chance of a catch rises steadily with
flow: at 0.1 m³/s it is `r pc(at("size_mad", 0.1))` of the chance at `r rec$size_min` m³/s, and
at 5 m³/s it is `r n1(at("size_mad", 5))` times as high. It falls in a straight line on this scale
as gradient rises, and less steeply than with flow. Those two thresholds are where in and out
separate best on held-out groups, a cut across a slope, not a step in the curve.

Distance does bend. The chance is highest about `r n0(signif(peak_m, 2))` m from the river and
nearly as high at 300 m, `r n1(at("dist_to_Q3_m", 300))` times the chance at
`r km_d(rec$exc_d)`. Past a few hundred metres it falls: to `r pc(at("dist_to_Q3_m", 3000))` of
the chance at `r km_d(rec$exc_d)` by 3 km and `r pc(at("dist_to_Q3_m", 10000))` by 10 km. The
recommended distance sits on the way down, past the bend. Beyond about 10 km the band widens
and the curve is not to be read.

## What is the grade?

The yes-or-no rule says where chinook rear. The grade says how much use to expect. A segment's
grade is the curve's predicted chance of a catch on a standard electrofishing visit at the
segment's own size, gradient and distance to a river, with the group's own level left out so
grades compare across watersheds. It is divided by the chance that 95 % of accessible segments
fall below, `r format(meta$grade$reference_rate)`, and capped at 1. A segment at 1 is in the top
twentieth of the accessible network; a segment at 0.3 is expected to give a catch about a third
as often as one at 1. It is expected use, not habitat quality.

Across the `r meta$grade$groups` groups link classifies for chinook,
`r n0(meta$grade$graded)` of the `r n0(meta$grade$accessible)` accessible segments received a
grade; the rest have no modelled flow. The grade is the same under
either rule. What changes is which segments each rule keeps:

```{r grade-km}
cls <- c("0-0.2", "0.2-0.4", "0.4-0.6", "0.6-0.8", "0.8-1")
gk <- tibble(Grade = cls,
             `default km` = n0(unlist(all_row[paste0("default_km_", cls)])),
             `recommended km` = n0(unlist(all_row[paste0("tuned_km_", cls)])))
gk <- bind_rows(gk, tibble(Grade = "graded km (km × grade)", `default km` = n0(all_row$default_graded_km),
                           `recommended km` = n0(all_row$tuned_graded_km)))
knitr::kable(gk, align = "lrr",
             caption = paste("Chinook rearing km by grade under each rule, over all", meta$grade$groups,
                             "groups, and the km weighted by grade."))
```

The recommended rule draws `r n0(all_row$default_km - all_row$tuned_km)` fewer km, and
`r n0(all_row$tuned_graded_km - all_row$default_graded_km)` more graded km. It gives up
low-grade streams and takes on high-grade ones near rivers.

## What does it change on the ground?

Both rules were run through link's three stages on copies of every group link classifies for
chinook: the habitat test behind link's access gate, the hand-entered reaches, and the removal
of rearing with no spawning within 10 km. `default` here is that regeneration, not the flags link
has stored.

```{r km}
km_t <- tibble(` ` = c("accessible stream", "`default`", "recommended", "lost", "gained", "change"),
               km = c(n0(all_row$accessible_km), n0(all_row$default_km), n0(all_row$tuned_km), n0(all_row$lost_km),
                      n0(all_row$gained_km), paste0(n1(all_row$change_pct), " %")))
knitr::kable(km_t, align = "lr",
             caption = paste("Chinook rearing km under each rule over all", nrow(per_group), "groups."))
```

Across groups the change runs from `r n1(min(per_group$change_pct))` % to
`r n1(max(per_group$change_pct))` %, with a median of `r n1(stats::median(per_group$change_pct))` %;
`r sum(per_group$change_pct > 0)` of the `r nrow(per_group)` groups gain.

```{r change}
ch <- x$change |>
  group_by(direction, reason) |>
  summarise(km_all = sum(km), km_1 = sum(km[order == "1"]), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(direction != "lost", desc(km_all))
knitr::kable(transmute(ch, Direction = direction, Reason = reason, km = n0(km_all), `on order-1 streams` = n0(km_1)),
             align = "llrr",
             caption = "Why each km was lost or gained, recommended rule against `default`, over all groups.")
```

```{r change-words}
lost_size <- ch$km_all[ch$direction == "lost" & grepl("^size", ch$reason)]
gain_exc <- ch$km_all[ch$direction == "gained" & grepl("^exception", ch$reason)]
gain_exc_1 <- ch$km_1[ch$direction == "gained" & grepl("^exception", ch$reason)]
```

Nearly all the loss, `r n0(lost_size)` km, is streams wide enough for `default` that carry less
than `r rec$size_min` m³/s with no `r rec$exc_q` m³/s river within `r km_d(rec$exc_d)`. Most of
the gain, `r n0(gain_exc)` km, comes through the exception, and `r n0(gain_exc_1)` km of that is
on first-order streams, which `default`'s width test never admits unmeasured.

The Bulkley (`r meta$map_group`) shows both at once. There the recommended rule draws
`r n0(map_row$tuned_km)` km against `default`'s `r n0(map_row$default_km)`
(`r n1(map_row$change_pct)` %), losing `r n0(map_row$lost_km)` and gaining
`r n0(map_row$gained_km)`.

```{r map, fig.width = 4, fig.height = 13.8, out.width = "100%", fig.cap = paste0("The Bulkley (", meta$map_group, "): accessible chinook streams by rule, kept under both, lost (`default` only) and gained (the legend's \"tuned only\": the recommended rule only); the same streams by grade; and the floodplain shaded by the grade of the segment beside it. Line width follows stream order.")}
f <- tempfile(fileext = ".png")
knw_compare_map(seg, water, png = f, fp_cells = fp_grade, ncol = 1)
img <- png::readPNG(f)
grid::grid.raster(img)
```

In the first panel, the orange is whole tributaries that fall below the flow floor. Gains are
few here: short green reaches of small streams beside a river.

**Floodplain beside the habitat.** For the groups whose whole floodplain has been mapped, each
30 m floodplain cell belongs to its nearest segment, so hectares can be counted beside each
rule's habitat and weighted by that segment's grade.

```{r floodplain}
fpt <- x$floodplain |>
  group_by(rule) |>
  summarise(groups = n(), ha = sum(ha), graded_ha = sum(graded_ha), .groups = "drop")
fp_w <- x$floodplain[x$floodplain$watershed_group_code == meta$map_group, ]
by_rule <- function(d, r, col) d[[col]][d$rule == r]
fp_tab <- tibble(
  ` ` = c(paste("all", unique(fpt$groups), "mapped groups"), meta$map_group),
  `beside accessible stream` = c(n0(by_rule(fpt, "accessible", "ha")), n0(by_rule(fp_w, "accessible", "ha"))),
  `beside default` = c(n0(by_rule(fpt, "default", "ha")), n0(by_rule(fp_w, "default", "ha"))),
  `beside recommended` = c(n0(by_rule(fpt, "tuned", "ha")), n0(by_rule(fp_w, "tuned", "ha"))),
  `graded, default` = c(n0(by_rule(fpt, "default", "graded_ha")), n0(by_rule(fp_w, "default", "graded_ha"))),
  `graded, recommended` = c(n0(by_rule(fpt, "tuned", "graded_ha")), n0(by_rule(fp_w, "tuned", "graded_ha")))
)
knitr::kable(fp_tab, align = "lrrrrr",
             caption = "Floodplain hectares beside chinook rearing under each rule, and the hectares weighted by grade.")
fp_change <- by_rule(fpt, "tuned", "ha") / by_rule(fpt, "default", "ha") - 1
```

The floodplain beside the habitat falls by `r pc(-fp_change)`, more than the km. The streams the
flow floor drops are mid-sized ones with floodplain beside them, and the small streams the
exception adds bring little. Weighted by grade, it barely moves.

**Two checks on the result.**

```{r checks}
ck <- x$checks
fv <- ck[ck$check == "fdis_visits", ]
rate <- function(r, s) { v <- fv[fv$rule == r & fv$segment == s, ]; v$n_detect / v$n }
ob <- ck[ck$check == "bcfishobs_outside", ]
```

- On the `r n0(sum(fv$n[fv$rule == "default"]))` FDIS visits with a recorded catch or miss on
  accessible segments in all `r nrow(per_group)` groups, rivers included, chinook were caught on
  `r pc(rate("tuned", "rearing"))` of visits on the recommended rule's segments and
  `r pc(rate("tuned", "accessible_not_rearing"), 1)` elsewhere; on `default`'s,
  `r pc(rate("default", "rearing"))` and `r pc(rate("default", "accessible_not_rearing"), 1)`.
  The tuning chose its rule on visits from this same record, so this shows the rule does what it
  was chosen to do, not that it is right.
- Chinook records from other sources, which never scored a rule, fall
  `r n1(ob$lift[ob$rule == "tuned"])` times as often on the recommended rule's streams as its share
  of accessible km would give, against `r n1(ob$lift[ob$rule == "default"])` for `default`. These
  are presence-only records, so the check rewards a rule that concentrates on where fish are
  reported, not one that covers everything.

## What the recommendation is not

- **Not applied.** Nothing in link changes until its configuration reads the thresholds table.
- **Juveniles caught by electrofishing, on streams.** River polygons, wetlands and lakes keep
  `default`'s tests under every rule, and spawning is not part of it.
- **Separation, not extent.** The score prefers the rule whose in and out differ most. It does
  not weigh the streams it leaves out: `r pc(rec$raw_rate_out, 1)` of the visits outside the
  recommended rule caught chinook, against `r pc(dflt$raw_rate_out, 1)` outside `default`.
- **A cut on a slope.** No threshold sits where the curve bends, so a value next to the
  recommended one is nearly as good. The region gives the range.
- **Measured at the visit, applied at the segment.** The distance to a river was measured from
  each visit; link measures it from a segment's downstream end, so the applied rule is a little
  looser. The gradient was scored on Freshwater Atlas segments; link applies it to its own,
  finer ones.
- **One link run.** Every figure is on link run `r meta$link_run_uid`.
- **Not habitat quality.** The grade is expected use per standard visit.

## Where this goes next

link's half of the story, the rule drawn by link itself across the province, waits on its
configuration reading the thresholds table
([link#346](https://github.com/NewGraphEnvironment/link/issues/346)).
